I understand what Quotient.exact means -- that equality of two Quotients implies equivalence of ther representatives.

What I'm failing to understand, is how it is proved from the other axioms of Quot, which only gives you the converse and some other things.

I'm trying to cut and paste this from Core.lean into another file and observe goal context in Info View, as I try modifications.

What I think might resolve the mystery, is how to make the motive argument explicit in q.inductionOn Setoid.refl. I don't understand what motive is deduced.

section Exact

variable {α : Sort u}

private def rel {s : Setoid α} (q₁ q₂ : Quotient s) : Prop :=
  Quotient.liftOn₂ q₁ q₂
    (fun a₁ a₂ => a₁ ≈ a₂)
    (fun _ _ _ _ a₁b₁ a₂b₂ =>
      propext (Iff.intro
        (fun a₁a₂ => Setoid.trans (Setoid.symm a₁b₁) (Setoid.trans a₁a₂ a₂b₂))
        (fun b₁b₂ => Setoid.trans a₁b₁ (Setoid.trans b₁b₂ (Setoid.symm a₂b₂)))))

private theorem rel.refl {s : Setoid α} (q : Quotient s) : rel q q :=
  q.inductionOn Setoid.refl

private theorem rel_of_eq {s : Setoid α} {q₁ q₂ : Quotient s} : q₁ = q₂ → rel q₁ q₂ :=
  fun h => Eq.ndrecOn h (rel.refl q₁)

/--
If two values are equal in a quotient, then they are related by its equivalence relation.
-/
theorem exact {s : Setoid α} {a b : α} : Quotient.mk s a = Quotient.mk s b → a ≈ b :=
  fun h => rel_of_eq h

end Exact

The definition

private def rel {s : Setoid α} (q₁ q₂ : Quotient s) : Prop :=
  Quotient.liftOn₂ q₁ q₂
    (fun a₁ a₂ => a₁ ≈ a₂)
    (fun _ _ _ _ a₁b₁ a₂b₂ =>
      propext (Iff.intro
        (fun a₁a₂ => Setoid.trans (Setoid.symm a₁b₁) (Setoid.trans a₁a₂ a₂b₂))
        (fun b₁b₂ => Setoid.trans a₁b₁ (Setoid.trans b₁b₂ (Setoid.symm a₂b₂)))))

means the following: we say that rel q₁ q₂ if a₁ ≈ a₂, where q₁ is the class of a₁ and similarly for q₂. Here Quotient.liftOn₂ allows to define a relation like that. Now let's have a closer look at Quotient.exact:

theorem exact {s : Setoid α} {a b : α} : Quotient.mk s a = Quotient.mk s b → a ≈ b :=
  fun h => rel_of_eq h

so it is basically a restatement of rel_of_eq, that is

private theorem rel_of_eq {s : Setoid α} {q₁ q₂ : Quotient s} : q₁ = q₂ → rel q₁ q₂ :=
  fun h => Eq.ndrecOn h (rel.refl q₁)

where Eq.ndrecOn is

abbrev Eq.ndrecOn.{u1, u2} {α : Sort u2} {a : α} {motive : α → Sort u1} {b : α} (h : a = b) (m : motive a) : motive b :=...

so basically it says that if you have a term of type motive a and a = b then you also have a term of type motive b. In rel_of_eq you know that q₁ = q₂ and you see that the other argument is rel.refl q₁, that has type rel q₁ q₁. Here the inferred motive is fun q => rel q₁ q, so rel.refl q₁ has type motive q₁ and you get an element of type motive q₂ that is rel q₁ q₂ as required. This is the tricky one, in rel.refl the motive is simply fun x => rel x x.

section Exact

universe u

variable {α : Sort u}

private def rel {s : Setoid α} (q₁ q₂ : Quotient s) : Prop :=
  Quotient.liftOn₂ q₁ q₂
    (fun a₁ a₂ => a₁ ≈ a₂)
    (fun _ _ _ _ a₁b₁ a₂b₂ =>
      propext (Iff.intro
        (fun a₁a₂ => Setoid.trans (Setoid.symm a₁b₁) (Setoid.trans a₁a₂ a₂b₂))
        (fun b₁b₂ => Setoid.trans a₁b₁ (Setoid.trans b₁b₂ (Setoid.symm a₂b₂)))))

private theorem rel.refl {s : Setoid α} (q : Quotient s) : rel q q :=
  q.inductionOn (motive := fun x => rel x x) Setoid.refl

private theorem rel_of_eq {s : Setoid α} {q₁ q₂ : Quotient s} : q₁ = q₂ → rel q₁ q₂ :=
  fun h => Eq.ndrecOn (motive := fun q => rel q₁ q) h (rel.refl q₁)

/--
If two values are equal in a quotient, then they are related by its equivalence relation.
-/
theorem exact {s : Setoid α} {a b : α} : Quotient.mk s a = Quotient.mk s b → a ≈ b :=
  fun h => rel_of_eq h

end Exact

Thank you @Riccardo Brasca . I had figured out most of what you said. I knew that "magic" happens at q.inductionOn. But I didn't understand how such a simple motive works. What still puzzled me:

The motive of Quotient.inductionOn must map Quotient s to Prop. Indeed, rel x x : Prop.

However, the motive must also map Quotient.mk a to Setoid.refl for each a : α. I did not understand how the motive could take an opaque x and destructure it as Quotient.mk a !

So it the real magic that -- the proof that type a ≈ b in exact unifies with rel (Quotient.mk s a) (Quotient.mk s b) -- really happens from a lot of unfolding in exact? In context, it can look inside the complicated definition of the type generated by rel?

I'm still not satisfied with my understanding. Ultimately rel returns some function produced by the Quot.lift axiom.

I also don't understand how Quort.sound is involved.

Theorem Proving in Lean chapter 12 says: https://leanprover.github.io/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/#quotients

This is the axiom that asserts that any two elements of α that are related by r become identified in the quotient. If a theorem or definition makes use of Quot.sound, it will show up in the #print axioms command.

Of course, the quotient construction is most commonly used in situations when r is an equivalence relation. Given r as above, if we define r' according to the rule r' a b iff Quot.mk r a = Quot.mk r b, then it's clear that r' is an equivalence relation. Indeed, r' is the kernel of the function fun a => Quot.mk r a. The axiom Quot.sound says that ra b implies r' a b. Using Quot.lift and Quot.ind, we can show that r' is the smallest equivalence relation containing r, in the sense that if r'' is any equivalence relation containing r, then r' a b implies r'' a b. In particular, if r was an equivalence relation to start with, then for all a and b we have r a b iff r' a b.

I think what confuses you is the following: the various Quotient.lift things allow to define a function on the quotient F : X/∼ → Y (here I am using standard mathematical notation) given a function f : X → Y with certain properties. Now, of course F satisfies that F [a] = f a, but the subtle point is that this is not written anywhere in the Lean code! It is added as a "computational rule", so it's embedded in the kernel, it comes before any axioms. If you look at the doc for Quot.lift (that is the common ancestor of all of these declarations, and again it is not written anywhere in the Lean code) you see

/--
Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
quotient's relation.

Given a relation `r : α → α → Prop` and a quotient `Quot r`, applying a function `f : α → β`
requires a proof `a` that `f` respects `r`. In this case, `Quot.lift f a : Quot r → β` computes the
same values as `f`.

Lean's type theory includes a [definitional reduction](lean-manual://section/type-theory) from
`Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk r v)` to `f v`.

`Quot.lift` is a built-in primitive:
 * `Quot` is the built-in quotient type.
 * `Quot.mk` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
 * `Quot.sound` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`
 * `Quot.ind` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
   with `Quot.mk`; it is analogous to the [recursor](lean-manual://section/recursors) for a
   structure.
-/
add_decl_doc Quot.lift

If are wondering why, the only suggestion I can give is to try to add

opaque Quot {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Sort u

opaque Quot.mk {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Quot r

opaque Quot.lift {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Sort v} (f : α → β) :
  (∀ a b : α, r a b → Eq (f a) (f b)) → Quot r → β

opaque Quot.ind {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Quot r → Prop} :
  (∀ a : α, β (Quot.mk r a)) → ∀ q : Quot r, β q

and the axiom Quot.sound to your theory. At the beginning it works well, so there is no need to add this computational rule (that means that F [a] = f a holds definitionally). But when you prove functional extensionality (that is done via quotients) something very subtle happens, and if F [a] = f a is not definitional you are stuck.

Basically what happens is that you are trying to prove f = g given f x = g x for all x, and you use the fact that if f x = g x definitionally then you have f = (fun x => f x) = (fun x => g x) = g definitionally (here the first and last equality are eta (?) reduction)
(See #new members > Definitional equality with quotient types @ 💬 for a code example to play with the funext proof)

Aha! 

Lean's type theory includes a definitional reduction from
`Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk r v)` to `f v`.

I hadn't yet read that bit. I got as far as I quoted in Chapter 12 of "Theorem proving" and stopped and tried to fill in the gaps in the argument about Quotient.exact. With frustrations and finally a peek at the source and a cry for help.

So there is a real bedrock, built in rule of evalution here.

So Quot.sound isn't used to prove exact ? But rather, it is the converse, that with exact proves that the equivalence they call r'is precisely the equivalence closure of relation r.

I am not sure I understand the question, but in the proof of exact what is happening is that h has type h : Quotient.mk s a = Quotient.mk s b, so when you pass it to rel_of_eq you get rel (Quotient.mk s a) (Quotient.mk s b). We have to prove a ≈ b. Now it comes rel: it has defined as a property on the quotient giving when the property holds on element of α, via (friends of) Quot.lift, so, by the discussion above, you can replace rel (Quotient.mk s a) (Quotient.mk s b) by the property that has been used in defining ref, that is exactly a ≈ b.
I mean that rel (Quotient.mk s a) (Quotient.mk s b) is for the kernel identical to a ≈ b via this new reduction rule.
Note that in this case rel (Quotient.mk s a) (Quotient.mk s b) is a Prop, but this is irrelevant. The same works when building functions to, say, the natural numbers.

Right. If I may try to restate myself clearly.

universe u v
variable { β : Sort v }
variable { α : Sort u }
variable { r : α → α → Prop }
theorem lift_eval ( f : α → β )
  (h : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a = f b)
    : ∀ ( a : α ),
      f a = Quot.lift f h ( Quot.mk r a )
  := by
    intro
    rfl

That works! But I have read that the five axioms of Quot statable in Lean do not include this one. (The five give you the type contructor Quot, and value constructor Quot.mk, which is exhaustive by Quot.ind; and then lift and sound.)

I was puzzled, thinking that was either a missing axiom, or else somehow deducible from the others, and was vainly trying to prove it by more elaborate means.

But intro; rfl is enough. Why?

Now I see, the unquantified statement is given by its very own special _rule of inference_ of this formal system.

This rule of inference is crucial to prove Quotient.exact.

And as mentioned in "Theorem Proving in Lean" chapter 12, Quot.mk r a = Quot.mk r b determines an equivalence relation r' on α. Quot.sound says that the equivalence closure of ris contained in it. The theorem gives the opposite containment.

Therefore, r' is exactly the equivalence closure of r. Not some coarser relation -- which Quot.sound alone, without the inference rule, might leave as a possibility.

Paul Licameli said:

But I have read that the five axioms of Quot statable in Lean do not include this one.

Whether a proof of a = b is rfl or not in Lean is not expressible as an axiom. Axioms tell you that things are true, not why things are true or whether they are true "by definition" (i.e., by rfl). As another example, if we define a function on the natural numbers by recursion, by specifying that F(0)=37F(0)=37F(0)=37 and F(n+1)=F(n+1)=F(n+1)= (whatever) then the proof of F 0 = 37 is rfl and you will also not find an axiom about Nat.rec saying this.

Aah, I see that later on in your post you seem to have come to the same conclusion.

In fact it might be worth adding that if f a = lift f h (mk r a) were an axiom with some name Quot.lift_mk, then the proof would not be rfl, it would be Quot.lift_mk.

You are looking in the wrong place if you are looking for axioms explaining why something is provable by rfl. Where you should be looking is in the specs for definitional equality. See for example https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/ , where quotient reduction is explicitly listed as being something which is included in Lean's definition of definitional equality.

Thank you @Kevin Buzzard

As my gateway drug into Lean, I lately studied "The Little Typer," which you may know, and whose coathor @David Thrane Christiansen also wrote one of the Lean online reference books that I'm now enjoying.

That study included careful, repeated rereading of the appendix, and some playing with the minimalistic, dependently typed Pie language.

I'm trying to connect the notions and terminologies of Pie and Lean. So I think I get it, that "definitional equality" in the Lean docs corresponds with "sameness" in the Little book.

So in Lean, I understand now that the claim of our so-called Quot.lift_mk, which makes the theorem Quot.exact work -- is just given as unproven, not as an axiom, but as a rule of inference. That is even more basic than an axiom.

But still I don't understand, why it was a design choice in Lean, to make it a rule of inference and not an axiom! Is it a matter of efficiency? Or is it somehow even more powerful, logically, than an axiom would be?
you can't prove docs#funext unless it's a definitional equality :)

Paul Licameli said:

But still I don't understand, why it was a design choice in Lean, to make it a rule of inference and not an axiom!

#new members > Definitional equality with quotient types @ 💬

It's also a general practice in proof calculi to have lots of rules of inference and few axioms, going as far back as Gentzen. Hilbert style calculi with lots of axioms and few rules of inference are not practical
